## 1. What you'll build, and why

You've been building value types since concept 10 — structs, enums, optionals — and lowering
them to LLVM aggregates without ever asking the obvious question: *how big are they, and where
does each field sit?* This concept answers it. Given a type, compute its **size**, **alignment**,
**stride**, and the **byte offset** of every stored property — the same numbers `swiftc` reports
through `MemoryLayout<T>`, and for structs of scalars, *identical to the byte*. It's a short,
sharp lesson in the one rule that governs all of it: **natural alignment**.

This is Phase 3's layout chapter, written after the rest of the phase: it branches off
`13-optionals` rather than feeding concept 15, so nothing downstream depends on it.

- **You implement:** the struct padding walk and the field offsets.
- **Outcome:** `--emit-layout` matching swiftc's `MemoryLayout` on structs of scalars.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### Three numbers: size, alignment, stride

Every type has:

- **alignment** — the address multiple a value must start on (hardware likes aligned access; an
  `Int` wants an 8-byte-aligned address). A struct's alignment is the **max** of its fields'.
- **size** — the bytes from the start to just past the last field.
- **stride** — the size **rounded up to the alignment**: the distance between consecutive
  elements in an array. Size and stride differ exactly when a struct has trailing slack.

The single rule that produces all of them is **natural alignment with padding**: lay the fields
out in declaration order, and before each field, *pad* the running offset up to that field's
alignment.

### Why order changes size

The consequence is the lesson:

![Two structs, same fields, different order. `{Int; Bool}`: the Int fills bytes 0–7, the Bool sits at 8 → size 9, but stride 16 (rounded to the 8-byte alignment). `{Bool; Int}`: the Bool is at 0, then 7 bytes of padding push the Int to offset 8 → size 16. Same data, 16 vs 9 bytes — field order is a real performance knob.](figs/padding.png)

`{ var i: Int; var b: Bool }`: `i` at offset 0 (8 bytes), `b` at offset 8 (1 byte). Size = 9.
Alignment = 8 (the Int). Stride = round_up(9, 8) = 16.

`{ var b: Bool; var i: Int }`: `b` at offset 0, but `i` needs an 8-aligned address, so **7
padding bytes** push it to offset 8. Size = 16. The Bool's single byte cost the struct seven
wasted ones. (This is why C programmers reorder struct fields largest-first, and why Swift's
ABI documents field order as layout-affecting.)

Work `Three { var a: Bool; var b: Bool; var c: Int }` by hand and the whole rule falls out — a
running offset, padded up before each field, and a running maximum alignment:

| field | align | offset must be a multiple of | starts at | ends at | running align |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `a: Bool` | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| `b: Bool` | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 1 |
| `c: Int` | 8 | 8 | **8** (six bytes skipped) | 16 | 8 |

Size 16, alignment 8, stride 16; offsets 0, 1, 8. Those two columns — where each field *starts*,
and where the last one *ends* — are exactly `TODO(14b)` and `TODO(14a)`.

### Stride vs size, and arrays

Why two numbers? Because an array of `{Int; Bool}` can't pack elements 9 bytes apart — the
second element's `Int` would be misaligned. Stride (16) is the real spacing; size (9) is the
meaningful content. `MemoryLayout<T>.size` and `.stride` expose both, and the gap is where
"struct of mostly-Bools wastes memory" comes from. Nested structs compose by the same rule: a
struct field contributes its *own* size and alignment to the parent's walk.

### What the walk consumes: the shapes of a type

This concept adds no syntax — nothing new to lex or parse, and `--emit-layout` is the only new
driver mode. What it consumes is the **type**, so the recall is the set of forms `info_of`
dispatches on and the rule each one obeys. Four of the five are given; the `<-- yours` line is
`TODO(14a)`, and the offsets it walks past are `TODO(14b)`.

| `Types.ty` | size | alignment | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `TInt`, `TDouble` | 8 | 8 | one machine word; `MemoryLayout<Int>.size` is 8 on arm64 |
| `TBool` | 1 | 1 | a single byte — the reason padding exists at all |
| `TString` | 8 | 8 | a pointer in our model (swiftc's `String` is 16: a two-word struct) |
| `TVoid` | 0 | 1 | no content; its *stride* is still 1, so an array of them has distinct addresses |
| `TStruct n` | *the padding walk* | max of the fields' | **`<-- yours`** — declaration order, pad before each field |
| `TEnum n` | `8 × (1 + widest payload)` | 8 | a tag word plus payload words (§ below: swiftc packs it smaller) |
| `TOptional t` | `8 + size(t)` | 8 | `{ i64 tag, T }` — the enum rule, with one payload case |

And the two derived numbers, which are given: `stride i = max 1 (round_up i.size i.align)`, and
`round_up n a = (n + a - 1) / a * a` for a power-of-two `a`. Every layout question in the rest
of the course — an aggregate's `getelementptr` offsets, a class's header, a CoW buffer's header
— is this table plus one more row.

### How swiftc does it — spare-bit packing (the honest divergence)

Structs of scalars we nail exactly. **Enums and optionals we don't** — and the reason is the
most beautiful trick in Swift's layout. Our enum is `{ i64 tag, payload }` — a whole word just
for the tag. swiftc is cleverer: it finds **spare bits** in the payload (bit patterns the
payload can never use) and stores the tag *there*. The killer case: `Optional<SomeClass>`. A
class reference is a pointer; pointers are never `0` for a valid object; so swiftc represents
`.none` as the all-zeros pointer and `.some(ref)` as the pointer itself — `Optional<SomeClass>`
is **pointer-sized, zero overhead**, with `nil` == null. Our model would make it 16 bytes
(tag + pointer). swiftc's `MemoryLayout<Int?>` is 9 (a spare-bit case in the Int's high byte);
ours is 16. That's a documented divergence — and a glimpse of why real layout is a research
topic (`TypeLayout.rst` is dozens of pages). The principles you implement here are universal;
the packing is the optimization on top.

> Oracle: `swift/docs/ABI/TypeLayout.rst` (the spec — read the "Single-Payload Enums" and
> "Multi-Payload Enums" sections for the spare-bit machinery), `GenStruct.cpp`/`GenEnum.cpp`
> (the IR-level layout), and `MemoryLayout<T>` (the behavioral oracle you check against).

## 3. Build it, step by step

Everything is in `layout.ml`, and nothing else in the compiler changes. The dispatch in
`info_of`, the scalar/enum/optional rules, `round_up` and `stride` are given; two functions are
yours, and they are the same walk seen from two angles:

- **`struct_info`, `TODO(14a)`** — given the fields in DECLARATION order, produce the struct's
  `{ size; align }`. Each field's own `info_of` gives its size and alignment; the rule is the
  table in §2, and `round_up` is already written for you. Remember that a struct with no fields
  must still come out with a sane alignment. `layout-padding.t` and the alcotest group of the
  same name check it.
- **`field_offsets`, `TODO(14b)`** — the same walk, returning `(name, offset)` per field instead
  of only the total. If you find yourself writing the walk twice, that is fine for now; folding
  one into the other is Exercise 2's territory.

Neither function needs the module for anything but `info_of` (a field may be another struct, and
that is what `m` is threaded through for). Reference: `solution/layout.ml` — after you have
tried it.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase3-value-types/14-memory-layout
```

Every `.t` file calls `./lab.exe`, built from **this directory's** library, so the report is
about your code here.

- `layout-padding.t` — `--emit-layout`, the first hole: the scalar base cases, two `Int`s with
  no padding, the same two fields in both orders (16 against 9), size against stride, a run of
  `Bool`s, a nested struct bringing its own alignment, and the tagged-union sizes where we
  knowingly differ from swiftc.
- `layout-offsets.t` — `--emit-layout`, the second hole: offsets 0 and 8 with nothing skipped,
  the gap that padding leaves, consecutive `Bool`s, a nested struct at its own alignment, and
  padding in the middle of a mixed struct.
- Both cram files call the same driver mode, which prints sizes and offsets together, so they
  go green together. Per-hole reading lives in `test_layout.ml` (alcotest `layout`), whose
  `layout-padding` group calls `Layout.struct_info` and whose `layout-offsets` group calls
  `Layout.field_offsets` directly — fill `TODO(14a)` and the first group alone turns `OK`.
- `oracle.t` — **the headline**: for each of the 16 programs of `oracle-corpus.txt`, our
  `--emit-layout` output is turned by a small `awk` script into a Swift program that prints the
  same lines through `MemoryLayout<T>.size` / `.stride` / `.alignment` / `.offset(of:)`; swiftc
  compiles and runs it, and the two texts must be byte-identical. Because the probe is generated
  from our output, a missing line or an extra one fails too. It also builds and runs a struct
  with an optional field, and checks a `Double` multiply's IR — the two lowering fixes concept 13
  made, which this concept's compiler (and therefore `swiftml3`) carries.

A hole you have not started shows as `TODO` with the list of what it will check; a hole in
progress shows `FAIL` with, under each failing case, what the test wants and what your code
printed. On the untouched skeleton both cram layout files are `TODO`, `oracle.t` is `FAIL` (its
carry-forward cases pass, its corpus does not), and the alcotest is `FAIL` with `layout-scalars`
`OK`.

## 5. Benchmark it

Reorder a real struct's fields largest-alignment-first and watch the size shrink — then size an
array of a million of them. The byte you save per element times a million is the lesson:
layout is a memory-bandwidth knob, and `MemoryLayout` is how you measure it.

## 6. Exercises

1. **Single-payload spare bits.** Make `Optional<Bool>` size 1 (a Bool only uses `0`/`1`, so
   `2` is a spare value for `.none`) instead of `{i64 tag, i64}`. The simplest spare-bit case.
2. **Enum tag sizing.** A payload-free enum with ≤256 cases needs only a 1-byte tag, not a word.
   Compute the minimal tag size and shrink the layout — matching swiftc's `MemoryLayout<E>` of 1.
3. **`offset(of:)` for nested paths.** `\Outer.inner.field` — compose offsets down a key path.
4. **Reorder-to-pack.** A pass that sorts a struct's fields by descending alignment and reports
   the bytes saved — the optimization C does by hand and Swift's ABI permits the compiler to do.

## 7. Recap & what's next

Layout is one rule — natural alignment + padding — applied field by field: size is the end
offset, alignment the max, stride the size rounded up, and field order is a real size knob.
Structs of scalars match swiftc to the byte; enums and optionals are where swiftc's spare-bit
packing pulls ahead, which is the next layer of the same idea.

This closes the deferred Phase-3 layout chapter. Back in Phase 7, **31-stdlib-array-string**
builds `Array`/`String` on the heap — where these size/stride numbers stop being academic
(an array allocates `count * stride` bytes and addresses element `i` at `base + i * stride`).
